title: Nepal must build, but it must build smarter - OnlineKhabar English News
description: Nepal must build, but it must build smarter  OnlineKhabar English News
publisher.title: OnlineKhabar English News
full_article:
File: Construction works are underway for the Kathmandu-Nijgadh fast track.

Having grown up in London, I took its infrastructure for granted. It was only after moving to Cardiff University that I began to appreciate it. Although Cardiff was a developed city, it lacked the range of infrastructure I had become accustomed to in London. This contrast made me realise how deeply urban infrastructure shapes everyday life and highlighted the importance of balancing progress with resilience and sustainability, a theme I will explore throughout this essay.

For example, I had completely taken the London Underground for granted. Can you imagine being able to travel from the suburbs of London to Big Ben in just 30 minutes? Looking back, that was incredible.

While I was in Cardiff, however, I witnessed considerable infrastructure development across Wales. This became particularly apparent during my engineering studies, when local engineers discussed the Welsh Government’s plans to invest £3 billion from its capital funds in transforming the national transport network and making the energy supply greener. At the time, I was surprised by the scale of this investment, particularly given Cardiff’s susceptibility to severe storms. I now realise that sound policymaking requires a balance between immediate needs and long-term risks.

I remember studying for my exams when Storm Bert and Storm Darragh struck just weeks apart. These events brought home the significance of global warming, particularly as they coincided with my studies. During this period, my professor reiterated that, according to BBC News, the Earth was one degree Celsius warmer than the previous year. What struck me was that the engineering curriculum, particularly environmental engineering, emphasised preserving what we already have rather than pursuing innovations that could generate high carbon emissions.

What I found particularly interesting, however, was that while scientists and academics advocated phasing out environmentally damaging development, the Welsh Government appeared to take a different approach by pursuing rapid urbanisation. Nevertheless, it did not disregard all environmental recommendations. Much of its investment focused on green projects and renewable energy, including the Pembroke Power Station expansion, which aimed to enhance the UK’s renewable energy distribution.

This decision to prioritise certain forms of development over others reflects an attempt to reconcile economic growth with environmental sustainability. However, it also raises questions about the environmental risks governments are willing to accept in pursuit of immediate benefits and the potential long-term consequences if those risks are not properly managed. By targeting green energy projects, the Welsh Government appeared to acknowledge the importance of sustainable progress. Yet its strategy also highlights the complexity of policymaking in the face of climate change. One possible approach is to encourage development while rigorously integrating sustainable practices. Achieving this balance, however, requires continuous evaluation of potential trade-offs and a clear understanding of how present decisions might affect future resilience.

You might be wondering why I am talking about this. Recently, my father asked me to attend a webinar with environmental experts to analyse the catastrophic floods that struck Nepal over the past month. The Nepal-Tibet floods of 2026 reportedly caused more than 1,500 deaths, injured 9,300 people and left as many as 5,300 missing. The flooding was attributed to a massive glacier collapse and a rock avalanche.

One expert advocated an approach often supported by environmentalists: limiting environmentally damaging development and reconsidering whether the Himalayas can support large-scale infrastructure projects. He argued that Nepal could focus on alternative forms of development, given the significant environmental and geological consequences of building major infrastructure, such as a railway through the Himalayas. In his view, the risks might outweigh the benefits.

He also referred to the 2015 Gorkha earthquake, which exposed Kathmandu’s geological vulnerability. The city lies on a basin of relatively soft sediments, which can amplify seismic waves compared with solid bedrock. He argued that this makes it particularly important to account for Nepal’s geological risks when planning major infrastructure projects. Rather than concentrating on large new developments, he believed Nepal would benefit more from maintaining, strengthening and improving its existing infrastructure.

His argument was clear and, to be honest, quite challenging for someone as enthusiastic about development as I am. Nevertheless, he made a fair point. Geographically, Nepal faces significant challenges, with the Himalayas presenting considerable engineering difficulties. Although I did experience a natural disaster in Cardiff, it was not on the same scale as the disasters Nepal faces. I can therefore understand why environmentalists are cautious about large-scale urbanisation in Nepal. At the same time, I believe the country can continue building its capacity to respond to and mitigate such disasters through phased and carefully considered development.

As someone passionate about Nepal’s development, I remember meeting a girl from Chongqing, China, while I was at university. She told me that her home city was built across three layers, with trains running through and between buildings. Hearing her describe the city made me hopeful that London and Kathmandu, my two homes, would continue to embrace engineering innovation thoughtfully, improving everyday life while respecting their unique geographical and environmental challenges.

As a young person in my early twenties, I have always envisioned a world that prioritises comfort, accessibility and time efficiency, with these values reflected in the infrastructure we build. At the same time, I want engineering to be visually appealing without compromising functionality. I want every city to preserve its cultural identity while striving to become a smart city. After all, the true essence of a smart city was never about sacrificing the environment. It has always been about progressing alongside it.

I am tired of seeing traditional engineering approaches prioritise form over function while overlooking human-centred design. The future we were promised, and when I say “we”, I mean Gen Z and millennials, was depicted in Back to the Future , where engineering advancements made everyday life more exciting. We were promised flying cars, the abolition of lawyers, self-drying clothes, skyway traffic systems, weather control services, the Power Oasis and so much more.

The fact that engineering experts and environmentalists argue that countries should slow urbanisation raises concerns among those who regard innovation and progress as essential. However, after reflecting on these arguments, I have concluded that calls for restraint do not necessarily mean development should stop. Rather, they suggest that the development we pursue must be sustainable and resilient. I believe that when scientists and environmentalists call for reduced urbanisation, their intention is to encourage infrastructure that can withstand future challenges and environmental pressures, ultimately achieving a better balance between progress and sustainability.

In practical terms, I believe the time has come for Nepal to embrace engineering challenges and take bold steps forward, while ensuring that risk assessments and environmental impact assessments are integrated into every stage of the engineering design process.

My position is that Nepal should move forward with major projects such as the Nepal–China railway, but it must do so by incorporating sound engineering principles and nature-based solutions. Since the railway would pass through the Himalayas and Nepal’s mountainous terrain, construction activities involving mountain cutting and excavation could increase the risks of landslides, soil erosion and biodiversity loss. It would therefore be essential to incorporate bioengineering techniques for slope stabilisation, watershed and forest restoration, natural drainage management and ecological protection into the railway’s engineering design. These measures should complement conventional engineering solutions to minimise environmental impacts, reduce disaster risks and ensure the long-term safety, sustainability and resilience of the railway infrastructure.

Furthermore, major infrastructure projects often require substantial financial investment, potentially amounting to billions of dollars. For example, the proposed Nepal–China railway is estimated to cost approximately USD 8 billion, making effective project planning and management crucial to its successful delivery. Given the unprecedented scale and technical complexity of such a project, particularly in Nepal’s challenging Himalayan terrain, the potential for unforeseen challenges, cost overruns and implementation risks could be significant.

The use of advanced project management software and digital tools would therefore be essential to facilitate cost control, budget monitoring, resource allocation, risk management, construction scheduling and coordination among diverse stakeholders.

Moreover, integrating digital technologies such as Geographic Information Systems (GIS), remote sensing, satellite imagery and real-time environmental monitoring into the overall project management framework could play a crucial role in mitigating environmental risks. These technologies could help identify environmentally sensitive areas, landslide-prone slopes, biodiversity hotspots and vulnerable watersheds before construction begins. They could also support the continuous monitoring of environmental changes, including soil erosion, slope instability, water pollution, vegetation loss and habitat fragmentation throughout the construction process.

This would enable project teams to identify potential environmental problems at an early stage and implement appropriate mitigation measures, including bioengineering, slope stabilisation, watershed restoration and biodiversity protection.

Integrating these digital tools and environmental management systems from the initial planning and feasibility stages through construction and eventual operation would help minimise financial risks, prevent unnecessary environmental damage, reduce construction delays, improve decision-making and strengthen accountability among stakeholders. Ultimately, this proactive and integrated approach would contribute to more efficient project delivery while ensuring that economic development, environmental sustainability and engineering resilience remain central to the project’s implementation.

Ultimately, I do not want Nepal, or any other country, to fall behind in engineering development. This essay has sought to highlight that engineering development is fundamental to humanity, serving as a driving force behind economic progress, technological advancement and improvements in everyday life. Although the world faces increasingly unpredictable challenges, including natural disasters and environmental changes, I believe engineering development should not be viewed as a threat to the environment. Instead, it should be seen as an opportunity to integrate environmental and geographical considerations into the design and development of our infrastructure.

Reflecting on these challenges has encouraged me to think more critically about how we approach infrastructure development and the responsibilities that come with it. I do not believe Nepal should abandon ambitious projects such as the Nepal–China railway simply because its geographical landscape presents significant engineering challenges. Rather, these challenges should encourage engineers, policymakers and environmental experts to work together to develop innovative solutions that prioritise safety, sustainability and long-term resilience.

At the heart of this essay is my frustration with the tendency to put Nepal in a box when discussing engineering development. I do not want the country’s geographical challenges to become limitations that we, as stakeholders in its future, simply learn to accept. Nor do I believe engineering innovation should be restricted by the circumstances of the country in which it takes place. Instead, I want us to challenge conventional thinking and use engineering to reshape what is possible for Nepal.

Rather than allowing geographical difficulties to dictate the boundaries of our ambitions, I want them to inspire us to develop innovative solutions that demonstrate how humanity can overcome challenges intelligently. Ultimately, I want Nepal not merely to adapt to the limitations of its environment, but to help push the boundaries of engineering innovation itself.

title: Nepal Premier League financial transactions may exceed Rs 1.5 billion by third edition - Deshsanchar
description: Nepal Premier League financial transactions may exceed Rs 1.5 billion by third edition  Deshsanchar
publisher.title: Deshsanchar
full_article:
Kathmandu – The financial transactions of the Nepal Premier League (NPL) could exceed Rs 1.5 billion by its third edition, with franchises and business sectors increasingly involved in various capacities.

The commercial appeal of the NPL is enticing, with a significant number of spectators purchasing tickets to attend matches. Despite most games being scheduled between the Dashain and Tihar festivals, tickets have generally been sold out except for a few matches.

T-20 cricket is increasingly viewed as an entertaining format, where fans not only hope for their team’s victory but also revel in the thrill of sixes and fours. This excitement is palpable at the TU ground.

However, after 25 NPL matches, only nine teams batting first have surpassed the 150-run mark. In four innings, even 100 runs weren’t achieved. In the last five matches, the highest total in 10 innings was just 136 runs. Players have openly criticized the pitch, and spectators have also blamed the pitch and CAN. Although CAN has discussed the issue with the curator, results are yet to be seen.

At the Tribhuvan University International Cricket Ground, bowlers have dominated over batters. While high scores were recorded in the initial matches, batters have recently struggled to score. The inconsistency of the pitch, where sometimes a massive 217 runs are scored and other times teams are restricted to 83, 87, or 88 runs, has naturally raised questions.

For instance, Biratnagar Kings scored 83 runs against Kathmandu Gorkhas, Sudurpaschim Royals made 87 runs against Lumbini Lions, Janakpur Bolts were restricted to 88 runs against Chitwan Rhinos, and Pokhara Avengers managed only 97 runs against Lumbini.

The situation in the last five matches appears even more concerning. None of the teams in these 10 innings surpassed 136 runs, with three innings not even reaching 100 runs. On November 13, Sudurpaschim scored 125 runs against Kathmandu, who were then restricted to 118 runs. In another match, Janakpur was bowled out for 88 runs, while Chitwan lost six wickets chasing a target of 89 runs, indicating the difficulty of chasing even small targets.

Two contrasting scenarios have emerged at the same ground. On November 9, Pokhara Avengers scored 217 runs for the loss of three wickets in 20 overs against Karnali Yaks, winning by 63 runs. Similarly, Biratnagar Kings scored 186 runs against Karnali, and Kathmandu successfully chased a target of 181 runs against Karnali.

However, following these high-scoring games, low-scoring matches have become frequent, raising questions not only about the pitch’s condition but also its changing behavior during matches. The inconsistency, where batters sometimes find it easy to hit big shots and at other times struggle with even simple strokes, has sparked debate about the pitch’s uniformity.

Foreign players have prominently expressed dissatisfaction with the pitch conditions. Chitwan Rhinos’ experienced batter Ravi Bopara described this season’s pitch as the worst among the three NPL editions. Similarly, New Zealand all-rounder Jimmy Neesham criticized the pitch on social media, expressing his love for Nepal and the NPL but stressing the need for serious pitch improvements. He stated that a situation where 120 runs are sufficient for victory is unacceptable.

Chitwan’s David Malan also found the pitch challenging for batting, noting that the ball turns significantly in the first innings. Although batting becomes somewhat easier in the second innings due to dew, the conditions remain relatively difficult. Janakpur’s coach Shivnarayan Chanderpaul also mentioned that the wicket has not been conducive for batting since the start of the tournament.

The pitch conditions have altered teams’ strategies post-toss. Initially, most teams opted to bowl first, but recently, they have focused on batting first to defend totals. Of the 22 matches completed before November 13, teams winning the toss chose to bowl first in 17 games, winning seven and losing 10. Among the five teams that chose to bat first, two won. In the last three matches, teams have opted to bat first.

This shift indicates that teams are adapting their strategies according to pitch conditions. Sudurpaschim managed a 27-run victory over Janakpur despite scoring only 120 runs. On Friday, Kathmandu failed to chase a 125-run target. Another match between Chitwan and Janakpur was also low-scoring.

Low-scoring games are not always undesirable. Excellent bowling performances and competition until the final over can make T-20 cricket thrilling. However, the repeated scenario where batters struggle to play naturally and 120–125 runs are sufficient for victory poses a challenge to the tournament’s appeal.

There is growing interest in whether the remaining NPL matches will provide equal opportunities for both batters and bowlers. While the allure of T-20 cricket is not limited to fours and sixes, CAN needs to be aware that without competitive runs and balanced play, its commercial appeal could weaken.

title: Nepal calls for mountain-focused climate action at COP31 - The Kathmandu Post
description: Nepal calls for mountain-focused climate action at COP31  The Kathmandu Post
publisher.title: The Kathmandu Post
full_article:
Nepal has urged the international community to give greater priority to the climate crisis facing mountain regions, calling for dedicated action on mountains, fairer access to climate finance and stronger support for countries bearing the brunt of climate change.

These were among the key issues raised by Nepal’s delegation at the 31st Conference of the Parties to the United Nations Framework Convention on Climate Change (COP31), being held in Antalya, Türkiye, from November 9 to 20.

Foreign Minister Shisir Khanal, who led the delegation to COP31, returned home on Saturday while the conference continues through November 20. Minister for Agriculture, Forest and Environment Gita Chaudhary will lead the Nepali delegation for the remaining days.

According to the Ministry of Foreign Affairs, Nepal’s priorities at the conference included limiting global warming to 1.5 degrees Celsius, climate justice, protecting mountain ecosystems, adaptation, financial support for loss and damage, and strengthening multi-hazard early warning systems.

Addressing the conference’s opening session on November 9, Khanal drew attention to the devastating effects of recent climate-induced disasters in Nepal on people’s lives and livelihoods, infrastructure and ecosystems.

He called for a dedicated programme of work on mountains and climate change under COP31 and urged the inclusion of mountain-specific indicators in the Global Goal on Adaptation and the New Collective Quantified Goal on Climate Finance.

He also called for international support to address climate impacts stretching from the mountains to the sea, as well as for post-disaster reconstruction and recovery.

Speaking on behalf of the least developed countries (LDCs) at the Baku High-Level Dialogue on Climate Resilience on November 10, Khanal said countries that had contributed least to climate change were bearing a disproportionate share of its impacts.

He said adaptation must be recognised as an integral part of climate justice and that commitments to adaptation finance must translate into effective action.

Khanal and Chaudhary also attended the Antalya Summit on November 11.

At a high-level event on Early Warnings for All that day, Khanal said effective early warning systems were vital to protecting lives in mountain communities. He highlighted the need to collect data in high-altitude areas, expand satellite-based monitoring and snow surveillance, and disseminate warnings in local languages.

On November 12, Khanal addressed a high-level event titled ‘Advancing the Mountain Agenda’, jointly organised by Nepal, Bhutan, Kyrgyzstan, Pakistan and Tajikistan. He said the crisis facing mountains was a crisis for humanity as a whole.

Calling for mountain issues to be brought into the mainstream of global climate negotiations, he urged countries to make deep emissions cuts, provide climate finance through grants rather than loans, ensure swift and equitable support for loss and damage, and strengthen scientific monitoring of glaciers.

Nepal also joined Bhutan, Kyrgyzstan and international partners, including the International Centre for Integrated Mountain Development (ICIMOD) and the JOY Environment Network, in organising a high-level event on adaptation finance for mountain resilience.

Addressing the event, Khanal outlined the human, physical and economic losses caused by recent devastating floods in Nepal. He said adequate and easily accessible adaptation finance was essential to building resilience in mountain regions.

He also spoke at an event at the Nepal Pavilion on sharing experiences and strengthening regional cooperation to tackle transboundary climate-induced disasters in the Hindu Kush Himalaya region. He emphasised regional cooperation, technology transfer, the exchange of knowledge and experience, and partnerships among multiple stakeholders to address shared climate challenges.

On November 13, Khanal addressed an event on the climate finance needs of small island developing states (SIDS) and least developed countries. He called for predictable, accessible and grant-based climate finance to protect countries vulnerable to climate change and fragile mountain ecosystems.

Khanal inaugurated the Nepal Pavilion at the conference venue on November 9. According to the ministry, the pavilion showcased Nepal’s climate ambitions, achievements in biodiversity conservation and community-level climate adaptation initiatives.

On the sidelines of the conference, Khanal held separate meetings with United Nations Secretary-General António Guterres, Ethiopian Foreign Minister Gedion Timothewos and Finland’s Minister for Foreign Trade and Development Ville Tavio. They discussed issues of mutual interest and concern.

He also joined a group meeting with Guterres and foreign ministers from least developed countries.

Khanal met officials of the Non-Resident Nepali Association’s National Coordination Council in Türkiye, including its president, Binod Poudel. He said the government was committed to addressing problems faced by Nepalis abroad, improving digital consular services, responding promptly to grievances, and promoting safe, dignified and productive employment.

He added that protecting the rights and interests of migrant workers, particularly women, remained a government priority.

The ministry said Khanal also spoke to national and international media outlets about Nepal’s participation and priorities at COP31, as well as current regional and international issues.

Between November 9 and 13, Khanal addressed the conference’s opening session, attended the Antalya Summit, spoke at six high-level and thematic events, inaugurated the Nepal Pavilion, held three bilateral and high-level meetings, joined a group meeting of LDC representatives with the UN secretary-general, met members of the Nepali diaspora and took part in media engagements, the ministry said.

The ministry said Nepal’s participation had helped draw attention to the specific climate challenges facing mountain countries. Nepal set out its positions on a dedicated programme of work on mountains and climate change, equitable access to climate finance, loss and damage, scientific monitoring of mountain regions, technology transfer, capacity development, early warning systems and regional cooperation.

title: Foreign Minister Shishir Khanal Returns Home After Leading Nepali Delegation at COP-31 - Ratopati
description: Foreign Minister Shishir Khanal Returns Home After Leading Nepali Delegation at COP-31  Ratopati
publisher.title: Ratopati
full_article:
Kathmandu. Foreign Minister Shishir Khanal returned home on Saturday after leading the Nepali delegation at the 31st Conference of the Parties to the UN Framework Convention on Climate Change (COP-31). He had left for Turkey last week to participate in the conference being held in Antalya, Turkey, and has now returned home after concluding his participation.

The Ministry of Foreign Affairs stated that Nepal prioritized issues such as the Himalayas and climate change, the goal of limiting global temperature rise to 1.5 degrees Celsius, climate justice, conservation of the Himalayan ecosystem, adaptation and financial assistance for loss and damage, and strengthening multi-hazard early warning systems at the conference.

Speaking to journalists at Tribhuvan International Airport upon his return, Minister Khanal said that Nepal actively strived to establish the agendas of Nepal and mountainous countries in the COP process during the high-level meetings of the conference. Expressing optimism about the outcome of the COP, he said, 'Discussions have been held at various levels from Nepal's side to establish the issues of mountainous countries; we are fully optimistic that this year's conference will address our agendas in some form.'

During the conference, Minister Khanal had demanded the establishment of a separate program of action on 'Mountains and Climate Change' and expressed the view that specific indicators for mountainous regions should be included in the global adaptation goal and the new collective quantified climate finance goal.

In this regard, Nepal, in collaboration with Bhutan, Kyrgyzstan, and international partner organizations ICIMOD and the Global Environment Facility, also organized a high-level program on adaptation finance for mountain resilience.

Meanwhile, the Ministry of Foreign Affairs informed that Agriculture, Forest and Environment Minister Gita Chaudhary will lead the Nepali delegation in the various meetings and negotiations to be held during the remaining period of the COP-31 conference.

title: Over 21,000 killed in road accidents in Nepal in nine years, yet authorities fail to act on investigation reports - The Star
description: Over 21,000 killed in road accidents in Nepal in nine years, yet authorities fail to act on investigation reports  The Star
publisher.title: The Star
full_article:
KATHMANDU: When a passenger bus travelling from Pokhara to Kathmandu plunged 200 metres off the road in Benighat Rorang, Dhading, on February 24, 19 people were killed. The home ministry formed a task force to investigate the crash.

The task force concluded that driver fatigue had caused the accident, as the driver had been unable to maintain control of the vehicle. It recommended introducing a system to manage driver fatigue, setting maximum working hours for drivers on night services and making rest breaks compulsory.

It also called for digital monitoring of public vehicles, improvements to road safety infrastructure, closer monitoring of night-time travel, and the installation of cameras and tracking systems in public transport.

None of these recommendations has been implemented.

Nearly two months later, on April 30, a vehicle travelling from Rukum East towards Jaljala in Rolpa crashed, killing 20 people.

The home ministry again formed an inquiry committee. Although the committee submitted its report, its findings were not made public. Police said the jeep crash was caused by several factors, including continuous rainfall, overloading and inadequate monitoring of vehicles.

On Thursday (Nov 12), 14 people, including the driver, were killed when a microbus crashed in Bhimphedi, Makawanpur. The vehicle, with a seating capacity for 11, was carrying 20 people. According to Makawanpur police, 13 passengers and the driver died.

Police suspect that overloading and the driver's long hours behind the wheel may have contributed to the crash.

A committee led by Shesh Kanta Poudel, assistant chief district officer of Makawanpur, has been formed to investigate the accident. It has been given seven days to examine the cause of the crash, the condition of the road and potential risks, and submit a report.

Such committees and task forces are routinely formed after major accidents. Their investigations repeatedly identify familiar problems: poor road conditions, driver negligence, long hours behind the wheel without adequate rest, unhealthy competition among drivers and vehicles carrying more passengers than their permitted capacity.

Yet, despite identifying the problems and recommending solutions, the reports are often shelved.

Stakeholders say road accidents are increasing rather than declining because the recommendations are not effectively implemented.

The government must take road safety seriously and make protecting human life its top priority to prevent such accidents from recurring, said Punya Prasad Sitaula (Saroj), president of the Federation of Nepalese National Transport Entrepreneurs.

Writing on Facebook after a microbus crash in Bhimphedi, he said the accident had raised serious questions about the safety, technical condition and operating standards of electric vehicles.

“On such matters, the government must act responsibly and sensitively,” he wrote. Road accident prevention, he added, was not simply a matter of fate but a responsibility of the state, requiring technical safety guarantees and collective accountability from all stakeholders.

According to Nepal Police, the country recorded 187,949 road accidents over nine years, from the fiscal year 2018-19 to mid-October of the fiscal year 2026-27. The crashes left 51,049 passengers seriously injured and killed 21,031 people.

One of the country's worst recent road disasters occurred on July 12, 2024, when a landslide carrying mud and debris swept two passenger buses off the Narayanghat-Muglin road at Simaltal in Bharatpur-29 and into the Trishuli river. Nineteen bodies were recovered. The two buses were carrying 62 passengers. Three people were found alive, while 40 remained missing in the river.

Three days later, on July 15, a six-member task force led by Home Ministry Joint Secretary Chhabi Rijal was formed through a ministerial decision to investigate the disaster.

The task force recommended a range of measures to reduce road accidents, to be implemented through the Ministry of Physical Infrastructure and Transport, now the Ministry of Infrastructure Development. These included drafting a new Road Safety Act, establishing a National Road Safety Council, formulating a national road safety policy, and preparing standards, codes and procedures related to road safety.

None of these measures has been introduced and implemented in line with the recommendations.

The report also called for standards based on road classification, mandatory crash barriers on hazardous roads, public disclosure of risk assessments for major highways, and the installation of streetlights and CCTV cameras at dangerous and strategically important locations along highways. These recommendations, too, remain unimplemented.

Asked why investigation reports prepared after accidents are not put into practice, Anand Kafle, joint secretary and spokesperson for the home ministry, said the recommendations often involved several government agencies.

“Once a report is received, the issues it raises often concern multiple agencies. The ministry forwards the recommendations to those agencies for implementation, while also carrying out measures within its own jurisdiction,” he said.

Kafle claimed that some investigation reports had been made public and their recommendations implemented. But he said the availability of resources at the agencies concerned could limit implementation, with some measures having to be accommodated within their regular budgets.

“Some recommendations concern policy reforms. The vehicle-related law is being revised through the Ministry of Infrastructure Development, and suggestions made in these reports are being considered while drafting laws and regulations,” he said.

Traffic police say speeding and driving under the influence of alcohol are also major causes of road accidents. Accidents increase when both drivers and passengers are in a hurry.

Former Additional Inspector General of Police Bhim Prasad Dhakal, however, says driver negligence is responsible for most accidents. He also points to poor road conditions and the failure to carry out technical inspections of vehicles.

“Accidents also occur because traffic rules are not followed,” said Dhakal, who spent much of his career working at the Kathmandu Valley Traffic Police Office.

With large numbers of people travelling home during festivals, the risk of accidents rises, he said. Traffic police, transport offices and the Department of Roads should therefore pay closer attention during these periods.

“Additional checks must be arranged, and those who violate the rules should be penalised on the spot,” he said. “Transport laws need to be revised. Because traffic fines are relatively low, some drivers seem to be careless.”

He also called for road improvements, regular vehicle inspections and greater caution when driving in adverse weather conditions. Although rules require two drivers on vehicles operating night services, he said the provision has not been fully enforced.

Section 104 of the Motor Vehicles and Transport Management Act, 1993, needs passenger vehicles operating long-distance services to have at least two drivers. It also says the transport operator or vehicle owner must ensure that the drivers take turns at the wheel every six hours.

The provision, however, is not being respected, and the agencies responsible for monitoring compliance appear to have shown little interest in doing so.

The failure to act on investigation reports after major accidents is a longstanding problem, said former Home Secretary Umesh Mainali.

“Task forces are formed to investigate major accidents and prepare reports, but there is no follow-up on the recommendations they make,” he said. Overloading, he added, continues to cause accidents.

The relevant authorities must ensure that vehicles carry only the number of passengers they are designed for and that only suitable vehicles operate on particular types of roads, he said.

“Passengers who have been waiting for a long time tend to board the first vehicle that comes along, eager to reach their destination. They often do not consider how crowded it already is,” Mainali said. “Drivers, meanwhile, keep taking on passengers without regard for the vehicle’s capacity. This is how overloading leads to accidents.”

He believes the failure to effectively implement investigation recommendations is giving rise to accidents.

“Vehicles must carry passengers only up to their seating capacity. Traffic police must enforce this strictly,” he said. - The Kathmandu Post/ANN

title: The hidden cost of Nepal’s rising public debt - OnlineKhabar English News
description: The hidden cost of Nepal’s rising public debt  OnlineKhabar English News
publisher.title: OnlineKhabar English News
full_article:
Photo by Markus Spiske on Unsplash

Developing countries have rarely found it easier to borrow, or harder to afford it. That is the paradox of the World Bank’s International Debt Report 2026 . The external debt of low- and middle-income countries rose 5.5 per cent in 2025 to a record US$9.4 trillion. Yet debt service rose for a fifth consecutive year, and the poorest, IDA-eligible countries paid rates last seen in the late 1980s.

Nepal sits on the favourable side of most of these trends. Read alongside the latest data from the Public Debt Management Office (PDMO), Nepal Rastra Bank (NRB) and the IMF, however, the report points to risks that headline ratios understate.

Global picture: easier access, costlier terms

Cost. Countries eligible for the International Development Association (IDA), the World Bank’s concessional window, including Nepal, paid an average of 8.2 percent on new private loans in 2025. Their premium over official lenders widened from 3.4 percentage points in 2016 to 5.5 points.

Crowding-out. Median debt service in IDA countries rose from about 15 percent of government revenue in 2000 to more than 40 percent, driven mainly by domestic debt.

Valuation. The dollar’s steepest fall in five decades, in early 2025, explains at least 28.2 percent of the rise in developing countries’ public external debt, inflating loans in SDRs, yen or euros even when borrowers repay on schedule.

Nepal’s external debt: sound structure, rapid growth

The World Bank puts Nepal’s external debt at US$11.87 billion at the end of 2025, up 12.3 percent in a year, more than double the developing-country rate. The stock has almost tripled since 2015.

The structure is a strength. More than 90 percent of public external debt is owed to multilateral lenders, led by IDA (US$5.07 billion) and the Asian Development Bank (US$3.46 billion). Bilateral lenders hold US$967 million, mainly Japan (US$399 million) and India (US$257 million). Exposure to private creditors is negligible. New official loans in 2025 averaged 0.7 percent interest, a 33-year maturity and a six-year grace period.

One caveat: the World Bank reports all external debt in dollars by calendar year; the PDMO reports public debt in rupees by fiscal year. On the PDMO measure, external public debt was Rs 1,598.80 billion in mid-October 2026, or 24.22 percent of GDP. Servicing it in the first quarter of FY2026/27 cost Rs 16.13 billion, of which only Rs 3.49 billion was interest.

The pressure point is domestic

Total public debt reached Rs 3,009.11 billion, or 45.59 percent of GDP, by mid-October, more than four times its FY2016/17 level. The IMF, using a different GDP base, puts it at 49.6 percent.

About four-fifths of the Rs 386.22 billion spent on debt service in FY2025/26 went to domestic debt. The FY2026/27 budget allocates Rs 417.88 billion to debt service, close to the Rs 431.1 billion for capital expenditure. Most is principal that will be refinanced: Rs 245.89 billion of this year’s planned Rs 410 billion domestic borrowing repays maturing debt. Interest is rising; former National Planning Commission vice-chair Prakash Kumar Shrestha estimates it absorbs about Rs 100 billion of revenue a year. The bigger exposure is rollover risk: treasury bills and development bonds, the IMF notes, mature far faster than external loans.

Views differ. PDMO chief Gopi Krishna Koirala calls the position satisfactory apart from currency effects; economist Dilli Raj Khanal warns rising repayments will force deeper cuts to capital spending.

Currency matters too: Nepal services external debt in foreign currency but budgets in rupees, and PDMO data attribute about Rs 167.75 billion of the debt to exchange-rate movements. Execution is weak: NRB reports only about a third of the capital budget was spent in the first 11 months of FY2025/26, so borrowing increasingly finances recurrent spending and maturing debt rather than new capacity.

Remittances: the buffer the ratios miss

Nepal’s external debt equals 224 per cent of exports of goods, services and primary income. Joint World Bank–IMF debt sustainability analyses note that export-based ratios breach their thresholds under an export shock but keep Nepal at low risk because remittances are exceptionally high.

Remittances reached Rs 2.36 trillion (US$16.19 billion) in FY2025/26, up 37.1 per cent and more than that year’s federal budget. Part of the growth reflects a weaker rupee: in dollar terms, inflows rose 31.9 per cent in the first nine months. The IMF puts reserves at US$21.8 billion, about 12 months of imports.

Merchandise exports were Rs 315.29 billion against imports of Rs 2,096.37 billion, and refined soybean oil, processed from imported crude, made up about two-fifths of exports. Excluding China, the report finds, FDI in developing countries grew only 5.3 per cent between 2011 and 2025, while remittances more than doubled. Remittances sustain consumption; FDI builds the export capacity that services debt. The IMF lists Middle East war spillovers among near-term risks, a concern for inflows reliant on Gulf jobs.

Debt, food and shocks

The report also links debt to nutrition. In calm years, debt had little bearing on the share of people unable to afford a healthy diet. During the shocks of 2019–21 and 2021–23, a doubling of the debt-to-exports ratio was associated with a 1.6 to 1.8 percentage point worse change in that share. Higher debt also coincided with greater reliance on food imports and, for staples, fruits, vegetables and animal-source foods, fewer suppliers. The report treats these as associations, not causal effects.

For Nepal, the indicator to watch is debt relative to exports, not GDP. Nepal imports all its petroleum, and India supplied Rs 1,210.6 billion of its Rs 2,096 billion import bill in FY2025/26. At stake is real progress: in lower-middle-income economies, healthy-diet unaffordability fell from 58.5 to 45.2 percent between 2017 and 2025.

Policy priorities for Kathmandu

The government’s Rs 2.124 trillion FY2026/27 budget bets on capital spending and tax reform, and the IMF projects growth recovering from 3.0 to 5.3 percent. Sustaining that without a heavier debt burden requires five choices.

Treat concessional finance as a scarce asset. Any commercial loan or first international bond should be weighed against the 0.7 percent Nepal now pays. Fix execution before borrowing more. Strengthen public investment management and enforce the National Project Bank guidelines, as the IMF advises. Manage domestic debt actively. Longer maturities, a deeper bond market and a published borrowing plan would cut rollover risk. Raise revenue, not just spending. Implement the Domestic Revenue Mobilization Strategy and rationalise tax expenditures. Build buffers and disclose fully. The report cites evidence that disaster losses are larger where public debt exceeds 50 percent of GDP, a level the IMF estimate for Nepal now approaches. It also urges full disclosure of state-owned enterprise debt and guarantees.

The UN has extended Nepal’s least developed country graduation period to November 2029. That buys time on trade support, not on fiscal arithmetic. Nepal is not in a debt crisis, but debt that has quadrupled in nine years, increasingly serviced through domestic borrowing, leaves less room than headline ratios suggest. The goal is not more debt but better financing: affordable, transparent and invested in growth.

title: India-Nepal Relations: Can Balendra Shah's Visit Reset Decades of Diplomatic Challenges? - Open Magazine
description: India-Nepal Relations: Can Balendra Shah's Visit Reset Decades of Diplomatic Challenges?  Open Magazine
publisher.title: Open Magazine
full_article:
Some friends of Nepal and India have suggested that Nepal could use its position as a buffer between India and China, becoming a bridge connecting the two economies. But given the degree of mistrust between India and China, this is highly unlikely. For India, though, a more effective (and pragmatic) response would be to improve its own quality of engagement with Nepal. Better access to its markets and a stake in its development, particularly infrastructure, will create more durable goodwill than its flagging of Chinese foray in Nepal. The open border and its historical connections are advantages, but these cannot be taken for granted.

The economic relationship seems to offer the most viable route forward. Nepal has tremendous hydropower potential, and looking at how India’s power needs are growing, this can work out well. There already are frameworks in place that look at Nepal exporting electricity up to 10,000MW over the next decade. Nepal is also using the Indian grid to supply electricity to Bangladesh. This works for the mutual benefit of both countries. The possibilities are immense, but these are often held back due to disagreements. For example, even after almost three decades of agreement, the Pancheshwar Multipurpose Project, envisaged under the Mahakali Treaty of 1996, has not been able to take off. It has remained stalled due to, among other things, inconsistency in approach and disagreements over cost-sharing—Nepal has proposed a 30:70 cost-sharing ratio, but India says it is willing to bear only 65 per cent of the cost.

There are similar difficulties in trade and connectivity. India is Nepal’s largest trading partner, but Nepal feels the relationship is heavily tilted towards India. Kathmandu has sought better access to its agricultural and manufactured products; it also seeks measures to make its international airports at Pokhara and Bhairawaha commercially viable. These matters have considerable political significance in Nepal, especially among the young people who have given Shah a chance.

Shah’s forthcoming visit will bring some of these issues to the negotiating table. According to media sources in Nepal, it seeks a financial package of around $2 billion for post-flood reconstruction. How New Delhi responds to this need from Nepal and on what terms will largely determine the intensity of the reset.

The observation about structural imbalance between the two countries is relevant here. Nepal cannot forget the 2015 blockade, for it remains a reminder of how economic dependence acquires a political meaning, especially during times of political upheaval. This is where New Delhi should give leeway to Nepal when it insists on autonomy; after all, that does not have to be automatically interpreted as hostility. For Kathmandu, it would be prudent to maintain a sustained engagement that is not prone to episodic hostility. As Rae rightly puts it, “Ask no favour and take no wish list along. Talk to the other side eye to eye as an equal counterpart.”

For Modi, too, currently grappling with how to engage domestically with its own Gen Z, the visit by Nepal’s prime minister offers an opportunity to establish a working relationship with a government that came to power by trampling on all bearings of old power dynamics. Historical connection and geography are good, but to translate it into political goodwill needs serious work. As Pankaj Saran, India’s former ambassador to Nepal and former deputy national security adviser, has argued, “the stakes are too high for both countries to allow individual incidents to derail the promise of a new relationship based on mutual respect and advantage.”

full_article: Kathmandu. CPN (UML) Chairman KP Sharma Oli has commented that the Nepal Police organization is currently divided into two parts. Addressing the party's Bagmati Province Committee meeting, he claimed that the police have reached a divided state, where they are either beaten or left to watch. He mentioned that the current government is unnecessarily interfering politically in the police organization and stated that the police, bureaucracy, entrepreneurs, and businessmen are all dissatisfied with the current government's style of work. Accusing the government of working with political prejudice, Oli claimed that he was arrested on the day the government was formed as an act of revenge. He claimed that the police used brutal force on UML leaders and cadres who protested peacefully against his arrest, and stated that although the UML-led government in the past contributed to improving the police's service, facilities, uniform, and working environment, the current behavior of the police seems strange. Raising questions about the relationship between the government and middlemen, he said, 'Currently, the police are divided into two parts, one to be beaten and the other to watch. The government is creating a spectacle by intimidating businessmen in the name of money laundering and by bringing forward middlemen like Inam Sapkota.' Chairman Oli instructed the cadres to prepare for agitation and elections to re-establish the party's political influence. Mentioning that the two main tasks determined by the Central Committee are agitation and elections, he said that UML must re-establish itself among the public as a party with correct ideology, well-organized, and with a bright future. For this, all the party's mass organizations, professional, and community organizations must be actively mobilized, and no mass organization should remain inactive. Oli clarified that unconditional dedication is necessary for the cadres, stating that self-interest or conditions should not be attached to loyalty to the party. He mentioned that it is a matter of concern that the party organization has weakened in the Bagmati Province, where UML once had a strong hold, and said, 'To dispel the illusion that UML is finished, we must establish correct ideology and power through agitation and elections. To make Bagmati Province a model again and to educate the public who have blindly followed without looking at the background of political leadership, the youth must be mobilized extensively.' Oli accused that the public has recently been blindly following candidates and political leadership without evaluating their background, history, ideology, character, and economic conduct, like a crow in the fog. He expressed the view that it would be difficult to achieve political success if the youth are not organized into the party and advanced as active cadres, discussing that freeing citizens from such dangerous tendencies is the main responsibility of UML cadres.

title: Indian Railways approves weekly train service between Nepal's Janakpur Dham and Ayodhya - Connected to India
description: Indian Railways approves weekly train service between Nepal's Janakpur Dham and Ayodhya  Connected to India
publisher.title: Connected to India
full_article:
Indian Railways announces weekly train service connecting Janakpur Dham in Nepal with Ayodhya in Uttar Pradesh. Photo: Gemini AI Recreated

In a significant step towards strengthening cross-border connectivity between India and Nepal, Indian Railways has approved the introduction of a new weekly train service connecting Janakpur Dham in Nepal with Ayodhya in Uttar Pradesh, India.

The new service will establish an important rail link between two destinations deeply associated with the Ramayana tradition. Janakpur Dham is revered as the birthplace of Goddess Sita, while Ayodhya is regarded as the birthplace of Lord Ram.

The initiative is expected to provide passengers from both countries with improved access to these prominent religious and cultural centres while further strengthening their shared civilisational heritage.

Connecting key destinations across the border

Covering approximately 604 kilometres, the weekly train service will connect Janakpur Dham with Ayodhya Cantt., passing through several important towns and cities in Bihar and Uttar Pradesh.

The train will have commercial stoppages at Jaynagar, Madhubani, Shisho, Sitamarhi, Raxaul, Narkatiaganj, Gorakhpur, Basti, Mankapur and Ayodhya Dham, apart from its terminal stations.

The service will operate once a week, departing from Janakpur Dham on Saturdays and from Ayodhya Cantt. on Mondays.

Boost to religious tourism, trade and regional development

The new rail service is expected to make cross-border travel more convenient for pilgrims, tourists and other passengers. It will facilitate religious journeys between Janakpur and Ayodhya, promote tourism circuits associated with the Ramayana and improve mobility for people travelling for education, business and family-related purposes, according to an official government statement.

Improved rail connectivity is also expected to benefit local economies along the route by creating new opportunities for tourism operators, hospitality establishments, local traders and traditional artisans.

For communities in the border regions of Bihar and Nepal, the service will provide an additional passenger transport option while strengthening economic and social ties.

Strengthening India-Nepal friendship

India and Nepal share centuries-old cultural, historical and social bonds, with religious traditions and cross-border community relationships forming an integral part of their bilateral partnership.

The new train service will add another dimension to bilateral cooperation by leveraging railway connectivity to bring people and communities closer.

Through this initiative, Indian Railways aims to expand passenger connectivity while promoting regional tourism, supporting economic activity and reinforcing the enduring friendship between the two neighbouring countries.

title: Nepal for predictable, accessible, and grant-based climate finance - The Rising Nepal
description: Nepal for predictable, accessible, and grant-based climate finance  The Rising Nepal
publisher.title: The Rising Nepal
full_article:
Kathmandu, Nov 14: Minister for Foreign Affairs, Shisir Khanal returned home today after attending the 31st Conference of the Parties (COP31) to the United Nations Framework Convention on Climate Change (UNFCCC).

According to a press note issued by the Ministry of Foreign Affairs upon arrival of the Minister at Tribhuvan International Airport, the Minister had left here for Antalya of Turkiye last week as per the decision of the government (Council of Ministers).

Minister for Agriculture, Forest and Environment, Geeta Chaudhary, will lead the Nepali delegation to the Conference.

As the Ministry said, this Conference is one of the world's primary multilateral forums for defining shared policies, commitments, and courses of action to address the global challenges and impacts of climate change.

This conference has accorded top priority on limiting global temperatures rise to within 1.5 degrees Celsius, achieving the goal of net-zero carbon emissions by 2050, and strengthening the adaptive capacity and resilience of countries and communities affected by climate change.

The annual Conference being held since 1995 has provided a significant opportunity to take forward inclusive, effective and collective global climate action due to the participation of world's heads of the states and the governments, negotiators, scientists, private sector, youths and civil society representatives.

The Nepali delegation during the Conference called for ambitious mitigation through deep emission cuts aligned with 1.5°C goal; predictable, accessible, and grant-based climate finance—not debt—for adaptation and resilient infrastructure and sustainable livelihoods; and effective Loss & Damage arrangements with swift, direct, and equitable resources for frontline mountain communities. He also emphasized the urgency of robust science and multi-hazard early warning system with high-altitude glacier monitoring, satellite observation networks, and regional data sharing; political recognition of mountain-specific risks including under UNFCCC process; and stronger "Sagarmatha to the Sea" partnership linking mountain and ocean communities, alongside support for the proposed UN Decade for Mountain Resilience.

During his address to an opening plenary of the Conference on November 9, the Minister drew the attention of international community to the recent devastating disaster in Nepal, its severe consequences on people's life, livelihood, physical infrastructure and the ecosystem.

He also stressed the need to establish a dedicated Work Programme relating to ' Mountain and Climate Change' under COP 31, incorporating specific indicators of mountain region in the global adaptive goals and new collective quantitative climate finance target.

Similarly, Minister Khanal and the Minister for Agriculture, Forests, and Environment, Geeta Chaudhary, participated in the Antalya Summit held on November 11. Addressing a high-level event on "Early Warning Systems for All" the same day, Minister Khanal emphasized that an effective early warning system is indispensable for safeguarding the lives of mountain communities. He highlighted the need for data collection, satellite-based monitoring, snow/ice surveillance, and the dissemination of early warnings in local languages within high-mountain regions.

On November 12, during a high-level event on "Promoting the Mountain Agenda"—jointly organized by Nepal, Bhutan, Kyrgyzstan, Pakistan, and Tajikistan—he stated that when mountains face a crisis, humanity as a whole is at risk. Stressing the need to bring mountain issues into the mainstream of global climate negotiations, he called for significant emission reductions, climate finance based on grants rather than loans, prompt and equitable financial support for loss and damage, and scientific monitoring of glaciers.

During the summit, Nepal—in collaboration with Bhutan, Kyrgyzstan, and international partners such as ICIMOD and the Zoï Environment Network—also organized a high-level event on adaptation finance for mountain resilience. At the event, Minister Khanal briefed participants on the human, physical, and economic losses caused by the recent devastating floods in Nepal, and underscored the necessity for adequate and easily accessible adaptation finance to build resilience in the mountain region. Minister Khanal also addressed an event held at the 'Nepal Pavilion' concerning the exchange of experiences regarding transboundary climate-induced disasters and mechanisms for regional cooperation within the Hindu Kush-Himalayan region. He emphasized that addressing shared climate challenges requires regional cooperation, technology transfer, the exchange of knowledge and experience, and partnerships among multiple stakeholders.

On November 13, while addressing a session focused on the climate finance needs of Small Island Developing States (SIDS) and Least Developed Countries (LDCs), he underscored the necessity of ensuring climate finance that is accessible, predictable, easy to obtain, and grant-based—specifically to support countries affected by climate change and to conserve high-altitude Himalayan ecosystems.

Minister Khanal inaugurated the 'Nepal Pavilion' at the conference venue on November 9. According to the Ministry, the pavilion served as a platform to showcase Nepal’s climate ambitions, achievements in biodiversity conservation, and community-level climate adaptation initiatives to the international community.

During the conference, Minister Khanal held separate meetings with UN Secretary-General António Guterres, Ethiopian Foreign Minister Gedion Timothewos, and Finland’s Minister for Foreign Trade and Development, Ville Tavio. These discussions covered various issues of mutual interest.

Additionally, he participated in a collective meeting with the UN Secretary-General alongside a ministerial-level delegation representing the Least Developed Countries (LDCs).

According to the Ministry, Nepal’s participation in COP-31 has contributed to effectively presenting the unique challenges faced by mountainous nations due to climate change before the international community.

The Ministry further noted that Nepal articulated clear positions on several key issues, including: a dedicated work program on mountains and climate change; equitable access to climate finance; the effective addressing of 'loss and damage'; scientific monitoring of the Himalayan region; technology transfer; capacity building; early warning systems; and regional cooperation.(RSS)

title: Nepal's COP 31 Delegation Faces Diplomatic Setback in Antalya - Ratopati
description: Nepal's COP 31 Delegation Faces Diplomatic Setback in Antalya  Ratopati
publisher.title: Ratopati
full_article:
Kathmandu. It has been two and a half months since the raging floods of Bhote Koshi, Trishuli, and Budhi Gandaki swept away settlements, but tears have not stopped flowing.

Citizens whose homes were washed away by floods and landslides, who lost family members before their own eyes, and who are waiting for news of missing relatives, are still standing amidst the rubble today, searching for the state's real presence.

Since that catastrophic day in Bhadra, neither the victims have found reliable shelter, nor has the process of receiving basic relief and compensation begun due to the inability to legally confirm deaths. The Nepali government's jumbo team, which went to Antalya, Turkey, to demand climate justice on the international stage by showcasing the tears, suffering, and devastated geography of its citizens, has appeared unsuccessful in the forum of multilateral diplomacy.

The 31st Conference of the Parties (COP-31) to the United Nations Framework Convention on Climate Change, which began in 1995 and has been held annually to combat the serious challenges of climate change, is currently underway in Turkey. This forum has been active with the aim of drastically reducing greenhouse gas emissions, limiting global temperature rise to 1.5 degrees Celsius, and mobilizing financial assistance for least developed and geographically sensitive mountainous countries like Nepal.

Nepal had made a big publicity fanfare this time, intending to raise its voice strongly at the conference for climate justice, compensation for historical pollution, and unconditional grants. With this ambition, a jumbo entourage of dozens of ministers, members of parliament, political activists, and employees, including Foreign Minister Shishir Khanal, Finance Minister Dr. Swarnim Wagle, Minister of Agriculture, Forest and Environment Gita Chaudhary, Minister of Health and Food Sanitation Nisha Mehta, National Planning Commission Member Prof. Dr. Sanjay Acharya, Secretary of the Ministry of Forest Dr. Rajendra Prasad Mishra, and Member of Parliament Sagar Dhakal, landed in Antalya. However, the Nepali delegation's role was limited to formal speeches in plenary sessions, inaugurating a pavilion funded by their own resources, and tea gatherings.

Nepal's diplomatic defeat at the beginning of the Antalya conference was quite shameful. Nepal, along with neighboring Bhutan and the Central Asian country Kyrgyzstan, had submitted a proposal to establish a separate formal agenda on '1.5 degrees Celsius temperature rise and mountainous regions.' This proposal was put forward to establish the reality that snow is melting rapidly in the Himalayas, glacial lakes are on the verge of bursting, and downstream areas are facing devastating floods and landslides that are destroying the ecosystem.

However, the proposal, which the government had been trumpeting as an 'historic initiative' for months, was outright rejected in the preliminary discussions on the first day of the conference. Participants say that Nepal's leadership failed to understand the reality that multilateral international diplomacy is not a battle won merely by showing pictures of one's suffering and presenting a lament from the podium. 'Due to the lack of necessary preparation, lobbying with multilateral working groups, and political understanding to pass any formal agenda, Nepal's proposal did not even reach the main negotiation table,' a Nepali climate activist told Ratopati from Antalya.

The main technical reason for the rejection of Nepal's proposal was the extreme shortsightedness of the Ministry of Foreign Affairs and the Ministry of Forests. He claims that no concrete diplomatic dialogue was held with developed countries and groups of developing countries like G-77 before flying to Antalya. 'The European Union and other industrialized nations, fearing that giving separate recognition to mountainous regions would impose additional legal obligations and a huge financial burden on them in the future, vetoed Nepal's proposal in the very first meeting,' he said.

Nepal lacked any legal strategy or strong political alliance to overcome the resistance of developed nations. The ministries' officials, who were busy making lists of foreign trips while staying in Kathmandu for months, failed to understand the complexity of strategic issues to be raised on the international stage, leading Nepal to suffer a severe diplomatic setback before the world. The Nepali team was badly shaken in Antalya after its proposal was shamefully thrown out of the formal agenda. Later, the conference president, Murat Kurum, assured Nepal that two phases of 'Mountain Research Dialogue' would be organized in Bonn, Germany, in 2027 and 2028, and that Himalayan issues would be generally mentioned in the final declaration of the conference. Ministry officials publicized the symbolic consolation of two research seminars in Germany as a 'great achievement.'

Climate Finance Also Disappointing

The global reality of climate finance is equally disappointing. According to the UN's independent high-level expert group, developing countries will need US$200 to US$400 billion annually by 2030 just to cope with climate-related disasters. However, by 2026, only about US$822 million has been committed to the international loss and damage fund. Although there is international recognition that countries with high carbon emissions should pay compensation, there is a serious disagreement between developed and developing powers on who will pay how much.

While the US and other Western countries are evading responsibility for historical emissions, they are trying to shift the burden onto emerging economies like China and India. Mechanisms such as the Green Climate Fund, Adaptation Fund, and Loss and Damage Fund have become ineffective due to low budgets and complex bureaucratic processes. Although the Loss and Damage Fund under the United Nations recently approved a grant of US$20 million for flood-affected Nepal, it has proven to be 'a drop in the ocean' compared to damages exceeding US$5 billion.

Participants themselves say that the Finance Minister's advocacy for loans, admitting that it would be difficult to get even five to seven billion rupees in grants, confirms the government's complete failure, when overcoming such complex geopolitical and financial games requires strong scientific evidence and strategic pressure.

The Nepali delegation has been criticized for sending a negative message to the global community that they came to the Mediterranean coast merely for exhibition, entertainment, and photo opportunities, rather than for serious diplomatic negotiations. Participants argue that the activities inside the 'Nepal Pavilion' at the conference venue were not very fruitful. However, by securing a free space from the organizers, other countries also held programs and interactions at the Nepali pavilion.

Despite claims of organizing 4 dozen programs in the pavilion, no concrete international agreements were reached. 'Ministers giving speeches to their own staff, representatives of non-governmental organizations applauding within their own groups, and finally taking group photos to color social media – nothing meaningful was achieved,' says an activist who went to Turkey.

Jumbo Team's Antalya Tour, Technical Team Like a Travel Agency

The Climate Change Management Division under the Ministry of Agriculture, Forest and Environment, which was supposed to provide technical, legal, and policy leadership for the COP conference, transformed into a pure 'travel agency' during the preparation for the conference. Technical leaders like the Head of Division Dr. Maheshwar Dhakal and Deputy Secretary Deepa Oli spent weeks on logistical tasks such as arranging visas for hundreds of delegates, booking air tickets, booking hotels, and distributing travel allowances, abandoning the work of collecting scientific facts, preparing financial drafts, or building regional alliances necessary for negotiations.

Meanwhile, criticism is growing within the country as a large number of ministers and members of parliament, funded by public taxes, have gone to Antalya amidst such a major national disaster. Citizens have termed this trip of ministers and their entourages as a 'climate crisis' while flood victims are shivering under tents in the cold. Unable to bear this widespread public pressure and intense criticism on social media, Minister of Health and Food Sanitation Nisha Mehta hastily inaugurated the pavilion and returned to the country on the very first day of the conference. However, even though the Health Minister returned, the team of other ministers, National Planning Commission Member Dr. Sanjay Acharya, Secretary Dr. Rajendra Prasad Mishra, and Member of Parliament Sagar Dhakal, continued to enjoy themselves in Antalya. Chairman of the Infrastructure Development Committee, Ashish Gajurel, is just about to leave.

Foreign Minister Khanal's schedule includes addressing the 'Antalya Leaders Summit' and a high-level program of five mountainous countries at the COP-31 conference, which will run until November 20 in Antalya. Finance Minister Wagle is also scheduled to participate in various climate finance sessions, and ministerial-level political negotiations will take place on November 17-18.

However, the activist said that there is not much hope from the Nepali delegation, which has already lost its formal agenda on the first day of the conference, has shown a mentality of seeking loans instead of grants, and has lost the trust of its neighbors.
